title: Data: load, validate and snapshot the portfolio

blocks.text: 13.1.1 Data: Load, Validate and Snapshot the Portfolio

GridCap's planning team wants one tool in place of the dozens of scripts the course has written: a small **CIPT** (Capital Investment Planning Tool) that takes the planning export, builds the multi-period model, values every project, explains its answers, proves it repeats itself, and answers over HTTP. This module builds it, on GridCap medium (400 projects over the ten years 2027 to 2036), one milestone per lesson. Every milestone assembles code you already wrote in an earlier module, so each lesson names the lesson that taught each part and spends its words on how the parts fit.

The first milestone is the one every later one stands on: read the export, refuse it if it is wrong, and give the accepted inputs a name that never changes. GridCap is a fictional utility; its data is generated by the course, and no number in it describes a real company.
CIPT Lite Is One Program Built in Six Milestones
The tool is six library modules in `src/`, one per milestone, each importing only the ones before it:

rows: read the export, check every cell, cross-project rules, canonical digest, store
the model with every rule GridCap's data carries, named rows, the rule checker
NPV by start year, risk reduction from PoF and RUL, weighted value
pre-solve checks, a conflict and its planner message, why deferred
run manifests, the harness, properties, golden records, warm start
S3 snapshot and result store, SQLite job log, job API, frontier endpoint

blocks.text: The order is the order a request travels through the service: data, then model, then values, then the solve and its explanation, all of it repeatable, all of it behind an API. Each lesson's graded practice builds the same milestone on a small practice portfolio of its own, in the same shape throughout the module, so the practices too add up to one tool.

The export is the five CSV files and the `portfolio.json` that `gridcap.save_csv` writes (the course's `gridcap` package): one row per project, per start year's NPV, per asset, per budget and per crew limit. It is the shape a planning database's export has, and like any export it can be wrong in ways the model would never notice.
Read Every Cell and Keep Every Problem

`gridcap.load_csv` trusts its files: a cost typed `1,200` stops it with a `ValueError` at the first bad row, and a misspelt region goes straight into the model. The milestone's reader checks each cell as it converts it and records a **finding** (a rule, a severity, a subject and a detail) instead of raising, the pattern of lesson 1.3.2's row validator:

Every column gets the check its meaning calls for, read off the model's parameters as lesson 12.2.1 reads a schema: costs and crew-months are whole numbers (money is whole $k), programs and regions come from a known list, a project's window must fit the horizon with all its years of work (lesson 6.4.1), every start year in the window needs an NPV, and every parent and asset id must name a row that exists. Only when no cell has an error does the reader build a `Portfolio`.
`planted_defects.py` writes GridCap medium's export and plants six mistakes an export really makes, one at a time:

P010 cost typed with a comma         -> not-a-whole-number      P010           cost = '1,200'
P020 region misspelt                 -> unknown-code            P020           region = 'Vally'
P030 window reversed                 -> empty-window            P030           starts 2036-2034 with 3 year(s) of work in 2027-2036
P040 parent retired                  -> unknown-parent          P040           parent = 'P999'
P050 and P051 each other's parent    -> parent-cycle            P050 -> P051 -> P050 a project cannot be its own ancestor
2029 budget typed 391                -> must-spend-over-budget  2029           must-do work spends at least $880k; the budget is $391k

Each defect is refused with a sentence a planner can act on: which row, which column, what it holds. The first four are cell problems. The last two pass every cell check, because every cell in them is a valid value on its own; they need the next stage.
Rules Across Projects Run Only on Clean Cells

A parent cycle is two valid parent ids that point at each other. A budget of 391 is a valid whole number. Only a rule that looks at several rows at once sees the problem, and lesson 12.2.2 calls those rules the **quality gate**. The milestone's gate has four: a project that is its own ancestor, a child whose parent cannot start early enough for any of its starts (an error for a must-do, a warning otherwise), two must-dos in one alternative group, and a year whose budget is below what must-do work has to spend in it whatever start years it gets:

The `min` over start years is what makes the rule **sound**: it never refuses a portfolio that has a plan, because no plan can spend less than that least amount (lesson 9.1.2). P097 is must-do and can start only in 2029, where it spends $880k, so a 2029 budget of $391k proves there is no plan.
The gate runs on a `Portfolio`, so it runs only after the cells are clean:
That ordering has a visible cost. With all six defects planted at once, the export is refused with the four cell errors only:

all six planted at once: refused with 4 errors
   not-a-whole-number      P010           cost = '1,200'
   unknown-code            P020           region = 'Vally'
   empty-window            P030           starts 2036-2034 with 3 year(s) of work in 2027-2036
   unknown-parent          P040           parent = 'P999'

The cycle and the budget typo are found on the next attempt, after the four are fixed. That is the right trade: a cross-project rule on unclean cells would follow a parent id that names no project, or add a cost it could not read, and report nonsense with an error's authority. So the reader reports every cell problem in one pass, and the gate reports every cross-project problem in one pass, and neither guesses.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Snapshot Is Named by the Hash of Its Canonical Content

An accepted export becomes a **snapshot**: the validated inputs, frozen and named by their content hash, so that every later run, manifest and result can say exactly which inputs it used (lessons 10.2.4 and 12.2.3). The name is the SHA-256 of the **canonical form**, one chosen way to write the validated content: projects and assets sorted by id, every key sorted, every float fixed to six decimals, no spaces.

def canonical(pf: Portfolio) -> bytes:
    """Validated content, one way: records sorted by id, keys sorted, floats fixed, no spaces."""
    tree = pf.to_dict()
    tree["projects"].sort(key=lambda p: p["project_id"])
    tree["assets"].sort(key=lambda a: a["asset_id"])

`snapshot_medium.py` puts the name to the test. It accepts GridCap medium, then exports the same content three ways and one changed way, and hashes the first export in two fresh processes with different hash salts:

GridCap medium: 400 projects, 382 assets, 10 years, 39 must-do
accepted with 0 warning(s); digest df4edafe8608

export                             digest
as written                         df4edafe8608
every CSV in reverse row order     df4edafe8608
discount rate 0.0700000001         df4edafe8608
P101 first-year cost $10k higher   2d173fe29605
as written, PYTHONHASHSEED=1       df4edafe8608
as written, PYTHONHASHSEED=2       df4edafe8608

Row order and a float's last digits do not change the content, so they do not change the digest; one cost $10k higher does. The digest is also the one the `gridcap` package pins for GridCap medium (`Portfolio.content_hash()`, `df4edafe8608…`), because that hash sorts keys and writes the generator's projects in id order too. The module's tests pin the full 64 hex digits, so a change to the reader or the canonical form that shifted a single byte would fail a test instead of quietly renaming every snapshot.
Medium has 400 projects and 382 assets: 18 pairs of alternatives (repair or replace) share one asset each.
The snapshot store keeps each snapshot once, under its digest, and checks the digest again on every read (lesson 12.2.3):

store: put twice -> same key True, files 1
read back equals the original: True
after an edit in place: refused, df4edafe8608.json no longer hashes to its name
From here on, every milestone receives a `Portfolio` that passed both stages, and a digest to quote.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **CIPT Lite is one program built in six milestones.** Data, model, value, diagnostics, trust, service: each a module of `src/`, each importing only the ones before it, each assembled from lessons you have done.

**Read every cell and keep every problem.** Convert each cell with a check that records a finding instead of raising; build the portfolio only when no cell has an error. Six planted defects, six sentences a planner can act on.

**Rules across projects run only on clean cells.** Cycles, unreachable parents, mandated alternatives and must-do spend above a year's budget need several rows at once; each rule is sound, and none runs on values that could not be read.

**The snapshot is named by the hash of its canonical content.** Sorted records and keys, fixed floats, no spaces: the same content gives `df4edafe8608` in any row order and any process, and a $10k change gives another name.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: a file that no longer hashes to its name
one problem: rule, severity (error or warning), subject, detail
a check that never refuses inputs that have a plan
validated inputs, frozen and named by their content hash
one chosen way to write a value, so equal values give equal bytes

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [Python `csv`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html) (`DictReader` hands every cell over as text, so every conversion is the reader's); [Python `hashlib`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html) (`sha256().hexdigest()`, 64 hex digits of the bytes given); [Python `json`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html) (`sort_keys`, `separators`, `ensure_ascii`, `allow_nan`).
Challenges

items: The gate's budget rule counts only must-do projects. A planner adds a `fix_start` override that requires P086 to start in 2027 (lesson 6.5.6). Which stage should know about overrides, and what would the rule then add up?
Two exports differ only in a project's `name`. Should their digests differ? Think of a report that quotes project names next to the digest.
The reader refuses a whole export for one bad cell. Write down one case where a planner would rather drop the bad project and solve the rest, and what the result must then say.

blocks.text: Design Note: Refuse Loudly, Never Repair Quietly

The reader could have "fixed" `1,200` to 1200 and `Vally` to Valley. It does not, because a reader that guesses turns a data problem into a plan problem that nobody can trace: the plan would be built on inputs no one exported. Refusing with a finding sends the problem back to the system that made it, and the snapshot that is finally accepted is exactly what the export said.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**planted_defects.py.** Plants six defects in GridCap medium's export, one at a time and all at once, and prints each refusal (*Read Every Cell*, *Rules Across Projects*). *Try:* Plant only the cycle and the comma typo together. Predict how many errors the first attempt reports.

**snapshot_medium.py.** Accepts GridCap medium, hashes four exports of it and two child processes, and stores the snapshot (*The Snapshot Is Named by the Hash of Its Canonical Content*). *Try:* Swap two columns of `projects.csv`. Predict whether the digest changes.
The milestone's library is `cipt_data.py`.
